title: Living at home in Dallas and the fight on the streetcar
summary: He always lived at home, and tells how he and his mother and brother fought Baylor football players on a segregated streetcar.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Growing up under segregation: schools, neighborhoods, Jim Crow

blocks.x: So when did you...when you had your first job and you did go out and this was still around Texas, were you still living at home, basically?

Yeah, I always lived at home. I never lived away from home in Dallas, in Texas. I always lived at home. Because I was taught and trained to be very, very faithful and respectful. I'm over-respectful now to people. When I say, 'Yes, ma'am' and 'no, ma'am,' people think I'm crazy. It's not that, it's just that I was taught that way. I remember one time...people used to see us, you know, the Price boys, and they would say, 'These nice boys and this little old colored lady.' So one time we went to visit a friend on a streetcar...had to go to another section of the city and when we got to the other section of the city, coming back we got on the streetcar. The streetcar would stop and you would have to get on the streetcar in the front, pay your fare, and then walk the left of the streetcar to the back of the streetcar. So my brother, mother and myself did that and there were some kids from Baylor University--football players--picked a fight with us. Well, they were sitting in the white section and we had to walk through, and then they tripped us and punched

my mother. Well, my mother was like, when you say "fight," she...it was all right with her, you know what I mean...and then we were right with her and we beat the hell out of all those football players on that streetcar. We jumped up and there was a sign-- they had signs--there was a sign setting at an angle, "Colored" on one side, "White" on the other. I jumped up and got that sign, boy, and I was beating guys... I think that they thought it would be just a little melee where "These niggers are going to run," and all that. But boy, we fought 'em, and the guy drove that streetcar fast as he could right down to the city hall. And do you know they let those people that beat us up, that jumped on us, they let them get away. (End of Side 1)
